claims.claim: Hindu traditions are a diverse family with no single founder, no single scripture, and no commonly agreed set of teachings; 'Hinduism' is a scholarly label for this family.
'Hindu' derives from Sindhu, the Sanskrit name for the Indus river and its region, and the '-ism' label came into general use in the nineteenth century in the colonial context.
Core concepts: dharma (duty, virtue, or right order), karma (action and its consequences, possibly across lifetimes), samsara (the cycle of rebirth), and moksha (liberation from that cycle).
The classical four aims of human life (purushartha) are dharma (virtuous living), artha (worldly success or prosperity), kama (pleasure), and moksha (liberation).

Many Hindus describe a supreme reality (Brahman) whose qualities and forms are represented by a multitude of deities; Brahma, Vishnu, and Shiva (the Trimurti) are one common scholarly organizing device; both polytheistic and monotheistic framings exist within the traditions.

The Vedas are the earliest corpus of Hindu texts (Sanskrit hymns and ritual prescriptions, long transmitted orally as shruti); the Upanishads are philosophical treatises; the Ramayana and the Mahabharata are the two great epics, with the Bhagavad Gita a dialogue within the Mahabharata.

Puja is a central practice of Hindu traditions: offerings (water, fruit, flowers, incense), images of deities (murtis), and repetition of prayers and mantras, performed at home shrines and in temples.

Diwali (the autumn festival of lights) and Holi (the spring festival of colours) are widely celebrated festivals, and pilgrimage to rivers and sacred sites such as the Ganges is an important practice.

Yoga is a group of physical, mental, and spiritual disciplines originating in ancient Indian traditions and aimed at calming and stilling the mind; modern forms of yoga are practiced worldwide, often mainly for exercise.

Hindu traditions are a living, global family: around a billion followers, most in India, with significant communities in Nepal, Sri Lanka, and Southeast Asia and diaspora populations in places such as the United States and the United Kingdom.
Bhakti, loving devotion to a personal deity, is a major strand within Hindu traditions, expressed through worship, song, and service and visible in contemporary practice and art.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Dating of the Vedas and the Upanishads
positions: SEP (Religion and Science, section 2.3): foundational texts including the Vedas and Upanishads composed ca. 1600-700 BCE
BBC Religions: the Vedas took their present form between 1200-200 BCE; major Upanishads largely composed 800-200 BCE
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson describes the texts' general character and says they were 'composed over many centuries,' attributing specific estimates to sources rather than asserting a single date.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Is Hinduism the world's oldest religion?
positions: OpenStax: Hinduism originated in the Indus River Valley about 4,500 years ago and is described as the oldest religion in the world
BBC Religions: 'In some ways Hinduism is the oldest living religion in the world, or at least elements within it stretch back many thousands of years'
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson avoids the strong claim and does not repeat 'oldest religion'; it says the traditions developed on the Indian subcontinent over many centuries.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Polytheism versus monotheism as a description of Hindu belief
positions: OpenStax: many Westerners view the multiple manifestations of Hinduism's godhead as polytheistic, while Hindus might describe those manifestations as a monotheistic parallel to the Christian Trinity
BBC Religions: it is too simplistic to define Hinduism as polytheism; most Hindus believe in a Supreme God whose qualities and forms are represented by a multitude of deities
SEP: there are both polytheistic and monotheistic strands in Hinduism
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson describes both framings as present and never adjudicates; it notes that outsiders' labels do not capture how adherents describe their own practice.

positions: BBC Religions: writers often refer to Hinduism as 'a way of life' or 'a family of religions' rather than a single religion
SEP: 'Hinduism' is an awkward catch-all phrase that denotes diverse religious and philosophical traditions
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson names the scholarly debate explicitly (one tradition with enormous internal diversity versus many related traditions under one name) and treats it as an open analytical question.

sourceRecords.title: 15.2 World Religions — Introduction to Sociology 3e
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A per the assignment brief. Read live via curl with a browser user-agent on 2026-08-21 (HTTP 200). Supports: roughly one billion followers making Hinduism the third-largest of the world's religions; origin in the Indus River Valley about 4,500 years ago in what is now northwest India and Pakistan; a divine power manifesting as different entities, with Brahma, Vishnu, and Shiva sometimes compared to Trinitarian manifestations; the Vedas as multiple sacred texts of hymns and rituals mostly in Sanskrit; dharma as duty corresponding with right actions; karma as consequences balanced cyclically in this life or a future life; the observation that outsiders call the multiple manifestations polytheistic while some Hindus describe them as a monotheistic parallel to the Christian Trinity. Facts synthesized; no OpenStax wording reproduced.
